title: Right speech
hook: no lying, no divisive speech, no harsh speech, no idle chatter (MN 117)

segments.voice: Yesterday: ahimsa, and your line, no harm meant. Did you catch one of those little films before it finished? Day three hundred sixty-five: a calendar year's worth of days on this path.

I'm five minutes away, typed by someone who hasn't left the house yet. A story about a coworker, told while she's out at lunch. A reply with a little edge on it. A long voice memo that could have been one sentence. None of these is a crime. Set side by side, though, they make a fairly complete map of how talk goes wrong, and the Buddha drew that same map in four lines. Right intention was the direction set inside. Today we reach the first factor of the path that comes out of the mouth: right speech.
screen: `I'M FIVE MINUTES AWAY.` → `UNTRUE, ABOUT SOMEONE, SHARP.` → `OR NEVER NEEDED AT ALL.`

segments.voice: Sammā vācā. Sammā: right, whole, complete. Vācā: speech, the voice. In the great forty sutta, the Buddha defines it with four abstentions. Abstaining from false speech. From divisive speech, the kind that splits people apart. From harsh speech. And from idle chatter. Four guards at the door of the mouth. Two things stand out. First, the five precepts lay Buddhists take name only one of these, not lying. Right speech asks for all four. Second, look at the last guard. Idle chatter, samphappalāpa in Pali, is talk that goes nowhere: words to fill a silence, gossip with no purpose, saying things only to be heard. And it sits on the same list as lying. That doesn't make small talk forbidden; many kind words are small. Some teachers put the test as purpose: is this going anywhere good? The same sutta does something else worth noticing. It sets right speech inside a circle. Right view recognizes wrong speech as wrong. Right effort works to let it go. Right mindfulness stays present while you do. So speech isn't mended by a rule alone; three other factors run around it. Why would a path to freedom spend a whole factor on talk? Because speech is where intention, last week's subject, first touches another person. You set the direction inside; now it comes out loud. And talk runs all day long, so the chances to practice do too.
screen: `SAMMĀ VĀCĀ: WHOLE SPEECH.` · `FOUR GUARDS AT THE MOUTH.` · `IDLE CHATTER MAKES THE LIST.` · `THREE FACTORS CIRCLE IT.` · then, large: `FOUR GUARDS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and rest. Let your mind replay the last day's talk, like scrolling back through your messages. Don't judge it; just sort. Was anything not quite true? Anything said about someone who wasn't there? Anything sharp? Anything said only to fill the quiet? Notice which guard was the sleepiest. Then let the replay go, and rest in the silence for a while, where no words are needed. After the bell, take that sleepy guard with you. The bell holds the time.
Sammā vācā. Right speech: no lying, no divisive words, no harsh words, no idle chatter. The third factor of the path.
Your line: four guards. Today, check your words as they leave: true, uniting, gentle, worth saying. Day three hundred sixty-five.

screen: `DAY 365 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FIVE MARKS OF GOOD SPEECH.`

howItsDone: Lay Buddhists take the fourth precept, not to speak falsely, often reciting it in Pali at the temple; right speech as a path factor adds abstaining from divisive, harsh and idle speech, and monastics keep detailed rules about speech in their discipline.

match.prompt: what's inside right speech: tap the pairs.

myth: idle chatter is on the same list as lying
MN 117 names four kinds of speech to give up, and idle chatter is the fourth.
right speech forbids all small talk
some teachers put the test as purpose: is this going anywhere good? many kind words are small.
the five precepts already cover all four parts of right speech
the precept names only false speech; right speech asks for all four.

fork.setup: a friend asks you to tell their boss they're sick. they're at the beach. which of the four guards is on duty?
fork.reveal: it's the first guard: abstaining from false speech, first of the four in MN 117, and the one the fourth precept names.

original.note: Pali sammā vācā: right, or whole, speech, the third factor of the eightfold path.

trapdoor: what you thought: right speech means don't lie.
what it means: four guards: no false, divisive, harsh or idle speech.
what a scholar hears: MN 117 describes right view, right effort and right mindfulness circling around right speech, so it's trained by three other factors, not by a rule alone.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 117 (Mahacattarisaka Sutta, the great forty)

notes: MN 117 paraphrased: four abstentions, and the circling of right view, effort and mindfulness around each factor.
MN 117 also gives a two-tier account (right speech 'affected by taints' and the noble, supramundane kind); omitted for simplicity.
'Thousands of words a day' is a general estimate (studies suggest roughly 15,000 or more); kept vague on purpose.

'Teachers often put the test as purpose' is a gloss, not a canonical definition of samphappalāpa (which the suttas describe as speech at the wrong time, not factual, not beneficial, not about the Dhamma or discipline).
Day 365 noted in the review as a calendar year of days.

Editor review: new hook (the old one sorted the day's words 'into piles', echoing day 360's two piles, duplicated the practice's replay, and claimed 'people who try this are often surprised... frequently it's the last one' without a source); dropped 'most lay Buddhists' and the unsourced 'thousands of words a day' (the note above about ~15,000 words no longer applies); 'teachers often' softened to 'some teachers'; pronunciation aligned with the other sammā days (SUM-maa).
